newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strike-hit German sweet firms back down on sick-pay.
newsitem.headline: Strike-hit German sweet firms back down on sick-pay.

text.p: Several German confectionary firms on Monday agreed not to implement a new law cutting workers' sick pay after strikes last week affected a number of factories around the country, including the Berlin plant of Swiss food group Nestle.

"Key plants are now hit by the trouble and if it carries on, it could hamper new ordering and block transport from products to grocery shops," said Karsten Keunecke, managing director of confectionery industry association BDS in Bonn.

Among firms which had now agreed to keep sick pay entitlements at 100 percent of salary was famous Aachen-based chocolates producer Lindt & Spruengli, officials at the NGG confectionery-to-restaurant sector trade union said.

They added that Lindt's works council had agreed to seek ways of reducing absenteeism in the firm in return for Lindt not implementing a new law that would allow it to cut sick pay to 80 percent of salary.
Confectionery-maker Biffar, based near the southern German town of Heidelberg, had also decided not to make the cuts to sick pay entitlements, the union said.
Confectionery workers are the first in Germany to hold all-out strikes against the deeply unpopular law cutting sick pay brought in by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in October.
Although only involving some 9,000 workers, the potential impact of the strike in an industry employing around 53,000 is great, particularly in the run-up to the Christmas sales season.

There have been much larger protests against the sick pay cuts by workers in Germany's key metal and engineering industries, but workers there are observing a rule banning all-out strikes for four weeks after the cancellation of worker contracts.
Some confectionery producers are now taking steps to have the strike declared illegal in their sector too.
Union officials did not say for how long the strike was due to carry on.
